reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant skeletal muscle sodium channelopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A (Nav1.4).
Episodes of flaccid weakness occur with a rising or normal-to-high serum potassium, in contrast to the low potassium of the hypokalaemic form.
Attacks are usually shorter and more frequent than in hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, often lasting minutes to a couple of hours.
Typical triggers are rest after exercise, fasting, cold exposure and potassium-rich foods.
Clinical or electrical myotonia, and overlap with paramyotonia congenita (also SCN4A), point away from the hypokalaemic form.
Onset is usually in the first decade, with normal strength between early attacks.
Respiratory and bulbar muscles are typically spared, and consciousness is preserved.
A fixed progressive proximal myopathy may develop in later life despite fewer acute attacks.
reference.pathophysiology: Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis results from gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A gene encoding the skeletal muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutations impair fast inactivation of the channel, producing a persistent inward sodium current that keeps the sarcolemma abnormally depolarised. Sustained depolarisation drives normal sodium channels into an inactivated state, rendering the membrane inexcitable so that action potentials can no longer be generated and the fibre becomes transiently paralysed. A rise in extracellular potassium further depolarises the membrane and precipitates or worsens attacks, whereas manoeuvres that lower potassium or repolarise the membrane tend to abort them.
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium measured during an attack
Electromyography with long and short exercise (McManis) testing
Thyroid function tests to exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Renal and adrenal function to exclude secondary hyperkalaemia
Creatine kinase and, where relevant, muscle biopsy
redFlags: Respiratory compromise during a severe attack
Findings suggesting a secondary cause of hyperkalaemia
reference.prognosis: Acute attacks tend to become less frequent with age and life expectancy is normal, but a proportion of patients develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy over the long term. Trigger avoidance and prophylactic therapy substantially reduce attack frequency.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the hypokalaemic form, in which the potassium direction and treatment are opposite, so misdiagnosis can lead to harmful management.
Overlooking myotonia or paramyotonia congenita overlap.
Failing to exclude secondary causes of hyperkalaemia before attributing paralysis to the primary channelopathy.
Provocative potassium loading carrying a risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia.
Attributing interictal proximal weakness to poor effort rather than an evolving fixed myopathy.
